newsitem.title: CANADA: Winds expected to test Winnipeg flood defenses.
newsitem.headline: Winds expected to test Winnipeg flood defenses.

text.p: Winnipeg braced for another test of its flood defenses on Sunday as forecasters predicted brisk winds that could weaken the dikes that have so far protected Manitoba's biggest city from rising waters.
The swollen Red River submerged a village on the outskirts of Winnipeg on Saturday, destroying about 100 homes, but flood barriers in the heart of the city were not breached.
Floodwaters swept through North Dakota and southern Manitoba, displacing 29,000 Canadians and 50,000 Americans, and were lapping at the edges of Winnipeg, a city of 650,000.

While the city has escaped flooding so far, officials worried that wind forecast for Sunday morning, and rain expected Sunday evening and Monday, will raise water levels and batter the dikes with waves.
"Waves can just be disaster for temporary dikes," said Larry Whitney, chief flood engineer for the province of Manitoba. "The worst thing that can happen is wind and wave."

A prime area of concern is a hastily built 25-mile (40-km) extension to a permanent dike southwest of the city. The structure is one of Winnipeg's main defenses and officials fear it might not hold. Derelict buses, oil booms and straw were brought in to hamper the effect of waves on the structure.
If the dike is breached, officials project that the bulk of the floodwaters will hit downtown Winnipeg in 40 hours.

The onslaught could be the last big test for Winnipeg, where the Red River crested on Thursday at 24.5 feet (7.5 metres) above winter ice level. The water should hold at that level until Tuesday or Wednesday before it starts to recede.
The flooding is the worst in the region since 1852. Four Canadians have died and property damage has been estimated at hundreds of millions of dollars in Canada and $1 billion in North Dakota.
The Red River swelled to 22 times its normal flow last month as record-breaking winter snow melted, flooding an area in southern Manitoba twice the size of Hong Kong.
The upscale community of Grande Pointe, home to about 325 people on the southeast edge of Winnipeg, was on Saturday the latest victim of the surging "Red Sea."
Emergency workers and Canadian troops ferried sandbags to the village in barges. About 100 of the area's 150 homes were under water and workers were trying to shore up dikes around the remainder.
"This is a last-ditch effort to save those homes," said Harold Clayton, executive coordinator of the provincial emergency program. "Our hearts go out to the people who have lost their homes."

The water level in the area was expected to rise a few more inches by Monday, but officials said homeowners would not be allowed into the area on Sunday to continue sandbagging because the winds would make conditions treacherous.

Despite the waters lapping at its flanks, Winnipeg has kept flooding at bay through a frantic campaign to strengthen dikes, erect sandbag barriers and pump water from areas where the defenses were leaking.

The city's savior has been a massive 29-mile (47-km) ditch known as the Floodway that splits the Red River as it enters Winnipeg. It diverts the waters around the city and was built after a devastating 1950 flood forced 100,000 residents from their homes.
